title: The Map of Ancient Philosophy: Animation Shows How Socrates, Aristotle, Confucius, the Buddha & Other Great Thinkers Fit Together
description:
in History, Maps, Philosophy |   	November 25th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve often fea­tured the charm­ing and info
body:
in History, Maps, Philosophy |   	November 25th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve often fea­tured the charm­ing and infor­ma­tive posters of Domain of Sci­ence. Each one maps out a dif­fer­ent field of knowl­edge: there’s biol­o­gy, physics, chem­istry, quan­tum physics, quan­tum com­put­ing, fun­gi, and many oth­ers besides. But with his lat­est map, Domain of Sci­ence cre­ator Dominic Wal­li­man has turned away from the sci­en­tif­ic realm — or rather, he’s ven­tured into the larg­er intel­lec­tu­al ter­ri­to­ry out of which it emerged. His new Map of Phi­los­o­phy, which he explains in the video above, includes schools of thought going all the way back to 600 BC, and thinkers from antiq­ui­ty like Thales, Laozi, Con­fu­cius, and the Bud­dha, who lived and died before sci­ence as we know it.
That hard­ly means that they’ve become irrel­e­vant today. There still exist soci­eties described as Con­fu­cian or Bud­dhist, of course, but in the West­ern world, we’re more like­ly to refer back to — and, in many cas­es, have read a bit of — the work of Socrates, Pla­to, and Aris­to­tle. “They basi­cal­ly laid the intel­lec­tu­al foun­da­tion of West­ern phi­los­o­phy, sci­ence, and polit­i­cal thought,” says Wal­li­man. (He also reminds us that it was Socrates who said that the unex­am­ined life is not worth liv­ing, which “hits pret­ty hard in the age of the dis­trac­tion econ­o­my.”)
Though often men­tioned togeth­er, these three ancient Greeks occu­py slight­ly dif­fer­ent posi­tions on the philo­soph­i­cal map, with Socrates clos­er to the land of ethics, Pla­to to meta­physics, and Aris­to­tle to epis­te­mol­o­gy.
As Wal­li­man explains, “epis­te­mol­o­gy stud­ies knowl­edge: what it is, where it comes from, and also how it dif­fers from faith or opin­ions,” while also seek­ing out its lim­its. Aris­totle’s rig­or in test­ing and orga­niz­ing knowl­edge makes him, in a sense, one of the ear­li­est sci­en­tists. Though his body of the­o­ry may no longer be our best means of under­stand­ing how the world works, his sys­tem­at­ic pur­suit of such an under­stand­ing set him apart from much of the ancient intel­lec­tu­al world. The islands off the coast of the map’s main­land rep­re­sent sub­fields still active­ly explored today, like the philoso­phies of mind, lan­guage, pol­i­tics, reli­gion, and sci­ence — which, for all its pres­tige, remains as sub­ject to philo­soph­i­cal inquiry as any oth­er area of human endeav­or. The map of phi­los­o­phy shows us not a rar­efied, most­ly aban­doned ter­ri­to­ry, but the place where we all live our lives, exam­ined or oth­er­wise.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: How a Thanksgiving Crisis Inspired the Invention of Swanson’s TV Dinner (1953)
description:
in Food & Drink, History, Technology |   	November 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment

body:
in Food & Drink, History, Technology |   	November 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sen­sa­tion of eat­ing and drink­ing — is a strange and com­plex and com­pli­cat­ed thing,” writes New York Times food edi­tor Craig Clai­borne. “I am con­vinced that there are a mul­ti­tude of peo­ple (Amer­i­cans, most­ly, to judge by the peo­ple who buy TV din­ners and frozen piz­zas) who have no taste what­so­ev­er.” That col­umn was pub­lished almost exact­ly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such con­ve­nience-ori­ent­ed food prod­ucts had already enjoyed promi­nence in Amer­i­can life for two decades. Though it could hard­ly have made a dent in the pop­u­lar­i­ty of TV din­ners, Clai­borne’s typ­i­cal­ly waspish aside did draw a let­ter of objec­tion from one Ros­alie Levine of Lake­wood, Cal­i­for­nia.
“I live alone, I must con­trol my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV din­ner’s price “can­not pos­si­bly be bet­tered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready din­ner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to pre­pare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up after­ward.” While none of these advan­tages were acci­den­tal, the oft-told sto­ry of the con­cep­t’s emer­gence begins with a cor­po­rate cri­sis.
“In 1953, some­one at Swan­son colos­sal­ly mis­cal­cu­lat­ed the lev­el of the Amer­i­can appetite for Thanks­giv­ing turkey, leav­ing the com­pa­ny with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it. “Inspired by the trays of pre-pre­pared food served on air­lines,” Swan­son sales­man Ger­ry Thomas set the machin­ery in motion to pack­age the unwant­ed meat with gravy and sides like corn­bread and sweet pota­toes, ready for stock­ing in Amer­i­ca’s frozen-food aisles.


	

The fol­low­ing year, Swan­son sold ten mil­lion such “TV din­ners,” a name attrib­uted to both the shape of the box­es and the form of enter­tain­ment fam­i­lies tend­ed to enjoy while eat­ing the meals with­in. “In 1950, only 9 per­cent of U.S. house­holds had tele­vi­sion sets — but by 1955, the num­ber had risen to more than 64 per­cent, and by 1960, to more than 87 per­cent,” writes Kovie Biako­lo in a more recent Smith­son­ian piece. (Among the Smith­son­ian Insti­tu­tion’s hold­ings, inci­den­tal­ly, is an orig­i­nal Swan­son TV din­ner tray.) Anoth­er break­through came with the intro­duc­tion of microwave-safe trays, bring­ing total prepa­ra­tion time under ten min­utes. Dur­ing the COVID-19 pan­dem­ic, Amer­i­cans rekin­dled their love affair with frozen meals, “spend­ing near­ly 50 per­cent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”
Where hol­i­day and com­mer­cial lore inter­sect, the details tend to get com­pli­cat­ed. Swan­son’s TV din­ner did have its prece­dents: the core tech­nol­o­gy for quick-freez­ing pack­aged foods was invent­ed over a cen­tu­ry ago by entre­pre­neur Clarence Bird­s­eye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remem­bers as “lit­tle cryo­genic mir­a­cles”), and in the late 1940s, dif­fer­ent com­pa­nies planned or attempt­ed to bring frozen meals to mar­ket under brands like Stra­to-Plates, FridgiDin­ners, and One-Eyed Eski­mo. None of those names tapped into the tech­nol­o­gy trans­form­ing not just Amer­i­can mass cul­ture, but also the Amer­i­can way of life. In the fifties, asso­ci­a­tions with tele­vi­sion (and, indeed, with air trav­el) car­ried a kind of sophis­ti­ca­tion they cer­tain­ly don’t have today. Per­haps Craig Clai­borne would be pleased that Amer­i­cans nev­er quite accept­ed microwaved TV din­ners as a sub­sti­tute for the Thanks­giv­ing meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is anoth­er mat­ter entire­ly.

title: The Illustrated Version of “Alice’s Restaurant”: Watch Arlo Guthrie’s Thanksgiving Counterculture Classic
description:
in Music |   	November 26th, 2026  2 Comments
	
			

	

Alice’s Restau­rant. It’s now a Thanks­giv­ing clas­sic, and some­thing of a tra­di­tion aro
body:
in Music |   	November 26th, 2026  2 Comments
	
			

	

Alice’s Restau­rant. It’s now a Thanks­giv­ing clas­sic, and some­thing of a tra­di­tion around here. Record­ed in 1967, the 18+ minute coun­ter­cul­ture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter with the law, start­ing on Thanks­giv­ing Day 1965. As the long song unfolds, we hear all about how a hip­pie-bat­ing police offi­cer, by the name of William “Obie” Oban­hein, arrest­ed Arlo for lit­ter­ing. (Cul­tur­al foot­note: Obie pre­vi­ous­ly posed for sev­er­al Nor­man Rock­well paint­ings, includ­ing the well-known paint­ing, “The Run­away,” that graced a 1958 cov­er of The Sat­ur­day Evening Post.) In fair­ly short order, Arlo pleads guilty to a mis­de­meanor charge, pays a $25 fine, and cleans up the thrash. But the sto­ry isn’t over. Not by a long shot.
Lat­er, when Arlo (son of Woody Guthrie) gets called up for the draft, the pet­ty crime iron­i­cal­ly becomes a basis for dis­qual­i­fy­ing him from mil­i­tary ser­vice in the Viet­nam War. Guthrie recounts this with some bit­ter­ness as the song builds into a satir­i­cal protest against the war: “I’m sit­tin’ here on the Group W bench ’cause you want to know if I’m moral enough to join the Army, burn women, kids, hous­es and vil­lages after bein’ a lit­ter­bug.” And then we’re back to the cheery cho­rus again: “You can get any­thing you want, at Alice’s Restau­rant.”
We have fea­tured Guthrie’s clas­sic dur­ing past years. But, for this Thanks­giv­ing, we give you the illus­trat­ed ver­sion.
If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!

title: A Sculptural Playground in Shanghai Is Designed for Human-Powered Play
description: In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in t
body:
In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.
“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art. In comparison to the artists’ earlier works, the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”
“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson, Marshmallow Laser Feast, and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram.

title: Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker's Captivating Photos
description: Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Her
body:
Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.
Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history. 

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.
In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.
The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria, and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram.

title: December 2026 Opportunities: Open Calls, Residencies, and Grants for Artists
description: Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never mis
body:
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly Opportunities Newsletter.
Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + PhotoFeaturedInnovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit. Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.
Bryson County Retreat FeaturedPracticing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.Deadline: Rolling.
Open Calls
Wildlife Photographer of the Year(International)Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.
Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art(International)The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for This Memory, a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead. Deadline: December 4, 2026.
Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab(Utah, National)Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.
Material Works Art Award 2026(International)Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.
Call for Mail Art(International)Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition love|mark, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.Deadline: December 15, 2026.
Sony Future Filmmaker Awards(International)The Sony Future Filmmaker Awards is a major program providing opportunities for creators and filmmakers. The shortlisted filmmakers are flown to Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City, California, to attend an awards ceremony and an industry immersion program. Categories include fiction, nonfiction, animation, immersive, student, and vertical format.Deadline: 7 a.m. CST on December 15, 2026.
GLEAM 2027 Request for Proposals(International)Olbrich Botanical Gardens in Madison, Wisconsin, invites proposals for temporary, large-scale, light-based artwork for GLEAM, a public art exhibition. The show will be open to the public from August 28 to October 23, 2027.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. CST on January 6, 2027.
Visual Arts Prize IDEA – Vila d’Amer(International)Apply for this inaugural prize open to artists working in all visual arts media. Two winning artworks, with prizes of €3,500 and €1,500, will become part of the permanent International Visual Arts Collection IDEA – Vila d’Amer.Deadline: January 10, 2027.
360 CHICAGO: CloudWalk Call for Artists(Chicago)One artist will be selected for this major installation in the CloudWalk gallery atop 875 N. Michigan Ave. The selected artist receives a $10,000 commission, and the winning installation will go on view starting April 2027.Deadline: January 18, 2027.
World of WearableArt 2027 Competition(International)Entries are now open for the 2027 WOW Competition in Wellington, New Zealand. Awards consist of NZ$200,000 in prizes, including the Supreme WOW Award of NZ$30,000.Deadline: February 11, 2027 (international), March 31, 2027 (New Zealand).
Grants
The Filmed in Nevada County Grant(International)To support filmmakers in the production of work in Nevada County, California, Nevada City Film Festival offers grants between $1,000 and $20,000.Deadline: December 1, 2026.
Southern Prize and State Fellowships for Visual Arts(U.S. South)The South Arts Southern Prize and State Fellowships acknowledge the highest quality artistic work being created in the American South. The program is open to individual artists living in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee. State Fellowships are $5,000, with one awarded per state. These then compete for two Southern Prize tiers of $25,000 and $10,000.Deadline: January 15, 2027 (fee waiver request by December 18, 2026).
The Virigina A. Groot Foundation Grants(International)Each year, the Virginia A. Groot Foundation offers three grants to artists who have exceptional talent and a demonstrated ability in ceramic sculpture or sculpture of diverse mediums. The grants are organized into tiers, with the top award providing $60,000, the second award offering $30,000, and the third awarding $20,000.Deadline: January 9, 2027.
Foundation for Contemporary Arts Emergency Grants(U.S.)Emergency Grants provide urgent funding for visual and performing artists and poets who have sudden, unanticipated opportunities to present their work to the public, but there is insufficient time to seek other sources of funding or unexpected expenses are incurred for projects close to completion. Each month, the organization makes approximately 15 to 20 grants in the range of $500 to $3,000 each.Deadline: Rolling.
National Lottery Project Grants(U.K.)Both individuals and organizations can apply to Arts Council National Lottery Project Grants. These awards are designed to focus on specific projects with starting and ending dates including festivals and carnivals, dance, libraries, literature, museums, music, theater, or visual arts programs. There is no maximum threshold for the fund.Deadline: Rolling.
Black Artists Grant(U.K.)The Black Artists Grant offered by Creative Debuts is no-strings-attached financial support to help Black artists. Selected applicants receive £500, and applications are reviewed monthly.Deadline: Rolling.
The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant (International)This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.Deadline: Rolling.
Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant (International)The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.Deadline: Rolling.
Residencies, Fellowships, & More
Kent Cultural Alliance Spring 2027 SERVICE Residency(U.S.)Artists are invited to apply for a six-week residency session in Chestertown, Maryland, devoted to the theme of service. Each selected artist will receive a $7,500 stipend for the six-week session, a travel reimbursement up to $1,000, and studio and gallery expense reimbursement up to $1,500.Deadline: 5 p.m. EST on December 1, 2026.
Charles Allis Art Museum Artist in Residence(International)Located in Milwaukee’s Lower East Side neighborhood, the Charles Allis Art Museum residency program gives one artist the opportunity to engage with the Allis’ collection of more than 800 historic pieces from the early 20th century. The participant receives an $1,800 honorarium and up to a $400 travel stipend.Deadline: December 4, 2026.
2026 McKnight Fellowships for Fiber Artists(Minnesota)Each year, the Textile Center awards two unrestricted $25,000 fellowships to post-emerging Minnesota fiber artists who demonstrate exceptional proficiency, sustained practice, and commitment to the field. Fellowship dates are March 1, 2027, to February 28, 2028.Deadline: December 7, 2026.
Open AIR Residencies(International)Open AIR is a Missoula-based nonprofit that brings artists and communities together through place-based residencies and public arts programs across Montana. Sessions currently accepting applications include summer 2027, fall 2027, and spring 2028.Deadline: December 7, 2026.
Cove Park Awarded Residencies for 2027-28(International)Located in beautiful Argyll & Bute, Scotland, Cove Park awards funded residencies, in addition to travel, visa, materials, and access allowances when required. (Self-funded Open Residencies and subsidized winter residencies are open on a rolling basis.)Deadline: December 11, 2026.
An Talla Solais Càirdeas/The Kinship Residency(International)BIPOC artists working in any medium are invited to apply to this fully funded residency in Ullapool in the Scottish Highlands. The program runs throughout January, February, and March 2027. The residency covers all work space, housing, mentoring, and exhibition costs in addition to a £750 weekly stipend.Deadline: December 14, 2026.
Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency 2027-28(International)Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency offers time and space amidst the natural beauty of Joshua Tree National Park. Seven-week residencies include scholarship funds, housing, and studio space designed to accommodate a broad range of artistic activity and open studio events. There is a $45 application fee.Deadline: December 15, 2026.
ren AiR(International)ren is a discovery platform where you share everything that goes into your artistic practice. For its residency, four selected artists will each receive $5,000 to develop and realize a project of their choice, wherever they are based, while sharing their creative journey with the ren community. In addition, eight artists will receive $2,000 prizes.Deadline: December 31, 2026.
Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship(International)The Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship offers twelve weeks to slow down and deepen your practice within a creative community. The program will welcome 18 fellows and is open to senior BFA students, MFA students, postgraduates, and artists with comparable professional experience.Deadline: January 7, 2027.
Fine Arts Work Center Seven-Month Residency(International)The Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown grants 10 annual fellowships each to visual artists and writers for a seven-month residency that runs from October 1 to April 30. Visual arts fellows are provided with a private furnished apartment and a separate studio, a $1,300 monthly stipend, plus a $1,000 exit stipend to support relocation at the end of the fellowship. There is a $55 application fee until midday on December 1, then $65 until the opportunity closes.Deadline: February 6, 2027.
Smithereen Farm Winter Residency(International)Smithereen Farm offers affordable, shared, winter housing to farmers and agrarian-adjacent people and creatives. In the winter, its studio spaces and rooms in shared houses are generally rented for $350 per month, which includes access to common rooms, space for studio work or desks, utilities, fast Wi-Fi at Reversing Hall, a carpenter shop, sewing machines, video projection space, and access to the farm’s agricultural library.Deadline: Rolling.
Jackrabbit Studios Residency(International)Jackrabbit Studios is a creative sanctuary and retreat space in the Southern California High Desert that welcomes creatives, healing arts practitioners, and facilitators at any stage of practice to our five acres of secluded and sublime desert expanse to craft a residency tailored to your season of practice. Fees range from $450 per week to $2,000 per week, and pets are welcome for an additional fee.Deadline: Rolling.

title: Lisa Marei Schmidt Appointed Director of Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee

body:
Lisa Marei Schmidt, the director of the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, is leaving her post to take over as director of the Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern, Switzerland, starting August 1, 2027. She will also chair the management board of both institutions and be responsible for their artistic direction. The Renzo Piano-designed Zentrum Paul Klee holds the world’s largest collection of works by Klee, while the Kunstmuseum Bern is Switzerland’s oldest fine art museum.

	Schmidt has been at the Brücke-Museum since 2017 and has orchestrated many exhibitions, including Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019), Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22), and Confiscated and Forgotten: The Female Artists Targeted by the Nazi ‘Degenerate Art’ Campaign, which opens April 30 to July 25, 2027. The Berlin museum is currently exhibiting Swedish Modernism until February 28, 2027, with a focus on the artist groups De unga (The Young Ones), De åtta (The Eight) and the Gothenburg Colorists. “To me, museums are places where art and people meet. They provide space for encounters, new perspectives and dialogue across society,” said Schmidt, in a statement on Thursday. “I very much look forward to getting to know the two remarkable institutions, the teams and the people in the City and Canton of Bern. Together, I hope to build on the Kunstmuseum Bern’s and Zentrum Paul Klee’s distinctive qualities and shape their future development.”
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Schmidt was chosen out of 97 candidates who applied for the position. Jonathan Gimmel, president of the umbrella foundation of Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee, said in a statement that Schmidt brings “remarkable professional expertise, international experience and a deep understanding of people” as she shapes the next “development phase of our museums.”

	Before joining Brücke-Museum, Schmidt was a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and a curator at the Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. She studied art history and modern German literature in Marburg, Amsterdam, and Berlin before graduating from the Royal College of Art.

schema.headline: Lisa Marei Schmidt Appointed Director of Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee
